lead: Scattering throws light out of the fiber core without absorbing it. Two linear mechanisms matter: Rayleigh scattering from density and composition fluctuations frozen into the glass, and Mie scattering from imperfections about the size of the wavelength. Rayleigh loss falls steeply as 1/λ⁴, so it sets the loss floor near 1550 nm and explains why early 850 nm systems needed short spans. Mie loss is weaker and is kept small by good fabrication. Every link budget uses these numbers; see Unit 5 for the budget itself.
prereq: You need: the attenuation coefficient and dB/km from Chapter 2.1, and where scattering sits beside absorption from Chapter 2.2.

sections.h3: The mechanism: light leaves the core

blocks.text: An optical fiber is not perfectly uniform. When silica glass cools, tiny regions freeze with slightly different density and composition from their neighbours. Each region has a slightly different refractive index. Light passing through sees a random array of weak index steps. Each step redirects a small part of the wave in another direction. Most of that redirected light leaves the core and is lost. The process is elastic: the scattered light keeps the same wavelength as the incident light. No energy goes into heat.

Rayleigh scattering uses fluctuations much smaller than the wavelength, roughly molecular scale. Mie scattering uses larger imperfections, comparable to the wavelength: rough core–cladding boundary, bubbles, unreacted particles or stress. Both are called linear scattering because the loss does not depend on the optical power. Raise the input power and the dB/km stays the same. Power-dependent scattering is a different topic; see Chapter 2.9.

The standard Rayleigh coefficient for a glass is given below. The exact constants differ with glass composition. The part to carry into an exam is α<sub>R</sub> ∝ 1/λ⁴. Double the wavelength and the Rayleigh loss falls by 2⁴ = 16.
α<sub>R</sub> = (8π³ / 3λ⁴) · n⁸ p² β<sub>c</sub> k T<sub>f</sub>
blocks.where: α<sub>R</sub> is the Rayleigh scattering loss coefficient; λ is the free-space wavelength; n is the refractive index; p is the photoelastic coefficient; β<sub>c</sub> is the isothermal compressibility; k is Boltzmann's constant; T<sub>f</sub> is the fictive temperature at which the glass froze.

blocks.text: Typical silica fiber numbers: about 1.9 dB/km at 850 nm, 0.34 dB/km at 1310 nm, and 0.17 dB/km at 1550 nm. These are consistent with 1/λ⁴ scaling. At 1550 nm, Rayleigh plus the infrared absorption tail gives the familiar floor near 0.2 dB/km. That floor is why long-haul links use the 1550 nm window, and why the same fiber is worse at 850 nm. Rayleigh is a lower limit for a given glass; better drawing cannot remove it because it comes from frozen disorder.

Imperfections of the order of the wavelength scatter by the Mie process. Sources include a rough core–cladding boundary, bubbles, unreacted particles in the preform, and stress. Mie loss has a weaker wavelength dependence than Rayleigh, roughly 1/λ² in the worst case, and sometimes almost flat over a short band. It is not a fundamental floor of pure glass. Good fabrication keeps it below the Rayleigh term in ordinary telecom fiber. A measured Mie term that is large usually points to a process problem, not to the glass itself.

Compare the two on a log plot. Rayleigh dives as wavelength rises; Mie falls slowly and stays low. At short wavelengths, Rayleigh can dominate strongly. At long wavelengths, the infrared absorption tail takes over. Between them lies the low-loss window.

figure.caption: Rayleigh loss falls steeply as wavelength rises, while the Mie term stays small; notice the 1/λ⁴ slope and the low loss near 1.55 µm.

spec.aria: Two curves of scattering loss against wavelength: the Rayleigh curve falls steeply as the fourth power of wavelength, while the Mie curve stays small and nearly flat.

examples.question: A silica fiber has a Rayleigh loss of 0.17 dB/km at 1550 nm and no measurable Mie term. (a) Estimate the Rayleigh loss at 1310 nm. (b) Estimate it at 850 nm. (c) The measured total loss at 850 nm is 2.5 dB/km; how much loss is left for other mechanisms? Use α<sub>R</sub> ∝ 1/λ⁴.
steps: Write the scaling: α<sub>R</sub>(λ) = α<sub>R</sub>(1550) × (1550/λ)⁴, with λ in nanometres.
(c) Other loss = 2.5 − 1.88 = 0.62 dB/km ≈ 0.6 dB/km. This is an upper bound on Mie plus absorption and other terms at 850 nm.
examples.answer: About 0.33 dB/km at 1310 nm, 1.9 dB/km at 850 nm, and 0.6 dB/km left for other mechanisms at 850 nm.

traps: Writing λ⁴ instead of 1/λ⁴: loss falls as wavelength rises, not rises.
Saying Mie scattering dominates an ordinary telecom fiber. Good fiber keeps Mie below Rayleigh.
Confusing scattering with absorption: scattering redirects light, absorption turns it into heat.
Mixing dB and dB/km. The coefficient is per kilometre; a 10 km span multiplies the dB loss, not the dB/km figure.
Treating Rayleigh loss as power-dependent. Linear scattering is fixed by the glass; stimulated scattering is a high-power effect in Chapter 2.9.

quiz.q: What is Rayleigh scattering in a silica fiber?
quiz.a: Elastic scattering by density and composition fluctuations frozen into the glass, with loss proportional to 1/λ⁴.

quiz.q: Why does Rayleigh loss fall as 1/λ⁴?
quiz.a: The fluctuations are much smaller than the wavelength. The induced dipole radiates with amplitude proportional to 1/λ², so the scattered intensity falls as 1/λ⁴.

quiz.q: A fiber has α<sub>R</sub> = 0.20 dB/km at 1550 nm. Estimate α<sub>R</sub> at 1310 nm.
Mie loss is 0.05 dB/km at 1.0 µm and follows 1/λ². Find it at 1.55 µm.
At 850 nm a fiber shows 2.5 dB/km total loss and 1.9 dB/km Rayleigh loss. What can you conclude about Mie scattering?
quiz.a: Mie plus absorption plus other terms is at most about 0.6 dB/km. Without more data you cannot separate Mie alone from absorption; the 0.6 dB/km is an upper bound.
The temperature at which the glass structure froze and stopped rearranging as the glass cooled.

quiz.q: Why is 1550 nm preferred for long-haul links?
quiz.a: Rayleigh loss is low there, the infrared absorption tail is still small, and erbium-doped fiber amplifiers work in that band. The result is a loss floor near 0.2 dB/km.

beyond: Not for the exam. Rayleigh scattering is also the basis of distributed sensing: an OTDR reads the backward scattered pulse to find breaks and loss along a link. Newer fibers attack the problem from the structure side: hollow-core and microstructured fibers guide light mostly in air, so the glass Rayleigh term is much smaller. Search terms: Rayleigh backscatter, OTDR trace, hollow-core fiber, fictive temperature.
